# Hardware Implementation and Validation {#sec-hardware}

A simulation runs with ideal clocks, ideal wires and a perfect master. The real question of this chapter is whether the node keeps its three main promises on real hardware. It should forward every word after a short and fixed delay, generate the PWM with the full 16-bit resolution, and answer the master correctly and in the order of the chain. To find out, the same bitstream was loaded into two GateMate boards connected as a short daisy chain, with a PC as the master, and all four serial lines were recorded with an oscilloscope.

The chapter follows the order in which the evidence was collected. It starts with the setup and the build (@sec-hw-setup, @sec-hw-flow, @sec-hw-results) and the PC master (@sec-hw-pc-program). It then shows the communication and the forwarding in the chain (@sec-hw-communication, @sec-hw-chain). The PWM and the driver stage follow (@sec-hw-pwm, @sec-hw-driver), and then the tests with broken packets (@sec-hw-robustness). It ends with the problems that came up and what they taught (@sec-problems).

## Hardware Setup {#sec-hw-setup}

Two boards are the smallest chain in which forwarding can be seen, because only then does a node pass data to a neighbour and receive an answer from it. The setup in @fig-hw-photo therefore has two GateMate evaluation boards, GM1 (serial number E1-32A0090) and GM2 (E1-32A0179). A PC with Python and pySerial [@pyserial] takes the role of the master and is connected to GM1 through a CP2104 USB-to-TTL adapter at 1 MBaud [@silabs_cp2104]. Each board drives four single 5 mm LEDs, red, green, blue and white, through BS170 MOSFETs on a breadboard [@onsemi_bs170], supplied from an external 12 V source. The signals were recorded with a PicoScope 4444, a four-channel oscilloscope with 12-bit resolution and 20 MHz bandwidth [@pico_4444_datasheet]. All measurements were taken at AES company in Bremen and the measurement equipment was provided by the company.

Both boards use the same Pmod pins (@tbl-wiring), because they run the same bitstream. This is the point of the design, because a node does not need to know its place in the chain. The grounds of the adapter and both boards are connected, and each board is powered over its own USB cable.

| **Pmod pin** | **Signal** | **Direction** | **GM1 is connected to** | **GM2 is connected to** |
|:-------------|:-----------|:--------------|:------------------------|:------------------------|
| 1            | `up_rx`    | in            | adapter TX              | GM1 pin 3               |
| 2            | `dn_tx`    | out           | adapter RX              | GM1 pin 4               |
| 3            | `up_tx`    | out           | GM2 pin 1               | open                    |
| 4            | `dn_rx`    | in            | GM2 pin 2               | open (pull-up)          |
| 7            | `seg1`     | out           | red driver              | red driver              |
| 8            | `seg2`     | out           | green driver            | green driver            |
| 9            | `seg3`     | out           | blue driver             | blue driver             |
| 10           | `seg4`     | out           | white driver            | white driver            |

: Wiring of the two nodes. Ground is connected between the adapter, GM1 and GM2. {#tbl-wiring}

The input `dn_rx` of GM2 stays open, because there is no third board. Its pull-up keeps it at the idle level of a UART line, so GM2 never sees a false start bit. The on-board LEDs D1 to D4 show the four PWM signals and D5 to D8 the lower four bits of the node ID. It gives a quick check of every test before the oscilloscope was connected.

![Prototype test setup. The PC sends the Flexlink packets through the USB-TTL adapter (CP2104) to GateMate 1. The two GateMate boards are connected through their Pmod connectors, one line for each direction. On the breadboard, one BS170 MOSFET (1) switches each of the four LEDs (2), which are supplied from an external 12 V source. The on-board LEDs D1–D8 show the PWM signals and the node ID.](images/ch6_setup_photo){#fig-hw-photo width=100%}

## Implementation Flow and Pin Constraints {#sec-hw-flow}

The whole flow from the Verilog file to both programmed boards is collected in one script, `build.bat`, so every build is repeated in exactly the same way (@lst-build).

```{.bash #lst-build lst-cap="Tool calls in build.bat (shortened)"}
yosys -q -p "read_verilog flexlink_node.v; synth_gatemate -top flexlink_node -nomx8 -luttree; write_json flexlink_node.json"
nextpnr-himbaechel --device CCGM1A1 --json flexlink_node.json --vopt ccf=flexlink_node.ccf --vopt out=flexlink_node.cfg --report utilisation.json
gmpack flexlink_node.cfg flexlink_node.bit
openFPGALoader -b gatemate_evb_jtag --usb-serial-num E1-32A0090 flexlink_node.bit
openFPGALoader -b gatemate_evb_jtag --usb-serial-num E1-32A0179 flexlink_node.bit
```

Yosys maps the design to GateMate cells [@cologne_toolchain], nextpnr places and routes it and writes the report `utilisation.json`, gmpack packs the bitstream, and openFPGALoader loads it over JTAG [@openfpgaloader]. The design is built once, and the same file goes to both boards, which openFPGALoader tells apart by the serial number of their USB interface. The bitstream is written into the volatile configuration memory [@cologne_ds1001], so the boards must be programmed again after every power-up. For a test bench this is an advantage, because a new version is loaded in seconds.

The constraint file `flexlink_node.ccf` connects the Verilog signals to the pins (@tbl-pins). The complete file, like all source code of this thesis, is available in the repository [https://github.com/snehashree499/thesis_sneha](https://github.com/snehashree499/thesis_sneha), in the folder `GateMate-FPGA-Projects/Flexlink_Node`. Each setting answers a problem of the setup. The inputs use a Schmitt trigger, so slow or noisy edges do not cause several switching events, and a pull-up, so an open input rests at the idle level. The outputs use a fast slew rate and 12 mA drive, for steep edges at 1 MBaud and for charging the MOSFET gates [@cologne_ds1001].

| **Signal**       | **Pin (bank)** | **Settings**                         | **Reason**                                       |
|:-----------------|:---------------|:-------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| `clk`            | IO_SB_A8       | Schmitt trigger                      | 10 MHz on-board oscillator                       |
| `up_rx`          | IO_NB_A0       | Schmitt trigger, pull-up             | clean edges, open input rests at idle level      |
| `dn_rx`          | IO_NB_A3       | Schmitt trigger, pull-up             | same as `up_rx`, open input on the last node     |
| `dn_tx`, `up_tx` | IO_NB_A1, IO_NB_A2 | fast slew rate, 12 mA drive      | steep edges at 1 MBaud                           |
| `seg1` … `seg4`  | IO_NB_B0 … IO_NB_B3 | fast slew rate, 12 mA drive     | drive the gates of the MOSFETs                   |
| `vref_2v5`       | IO_NB_A4       | 12 mA drive                          | constant high level for the driver stage         |
| `leds_n[7:0]`    | IO_EB_B1 … IO_EB_B8 | default                         | on-board LEDs D1 to D8                           |

: Pin assignment and I/O settings from the constraint file {#tbl-pins}

To make the results reproducible, @tbl-versions lists the tool versions and the source code version of the final build.

| **Item**                 | **Version**                                            |
|:-------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| OSS CAD Suite            | 20260920                                               |
| Yosys                    | 0.69+75 (git f0b945f63)                                |
| nextpnr-himbaechel       | 0.11.1-30 (git 3e53a0bf)                               |

## Implementation Results {#sec-hw-results}

The first check after place and route is whether the design fits and whether it is fast enough. @tbl-resources shows the resources from `utilisation.json`.

| **Resource**                  | **Used** | **Available** | **Utilisation** |
|:------------------------------|---------:|--------------:|----------------:|
| CPE logic (`CPE_LT`)          | 788      | 40,960        | 1.9 %           |
| CPE flip-flops (`CPE_FF`)     | 493      | 40,960        | 1.2 %           |
| General-purpose I/O (`GPIO`)  | 18       | 162           | 11.1 %          |
| PLL                           | 1        | 4             | 25 %            |
| Block RAM (`RAM_HALF`)        | 0        | 64            | 0 %             |

: FPGA resources used by the Flexlink node, as reported by nextpnr {#tbl-resources}

The node uses less than 2 % of the logic. The "available" values are twice the 20,480 CPEs, because nextpnr counts in half-CPE units, each with its own flip-flop (@sec-gatemate). No block RAM is needed, because the two FIFOs hold only eight words each and are built from flip-flops. This small size matters for the later goal of an integrated circuit, because the node is a very small block of logic, and the rest of a chip could be used for other functions or left out.

For timing, nextpnr reports a critical path of 14.54 ns, which gives $f_\text{max} = 1 / 14.54\ \text{ns} \approx 68.8\ \text{MHz}$. The design needs 50 MHz, a period of 20 ns, so every path arrives about 5.5 ns before the next clock edge. The critical path starts at bit 8 of the received word, the bit that marks a control word, and runs through four decoder levels to a register enable. Of its 14.5 ns, 11.3 ns are routing between the cells and only the rest is logic. A faster clock is not needed, because 50 MHz already gives the required PWM frequency and 50 clock cycles per UART bit (@sec-req-pwm-clock).

## PC Test Program {#sec-hw-pc-program}

In the AES system the master is a microcontroller. For the tests, a PC with a short Python program, `flexlink_pc_test.py` (in the same repository folder), takes this role, because it makes it easy to send any packet, also wrong ones. A PC serial port sends 8 data bits, while Flexlink needs 9 (@sec-9bit-uart). The program therefore uses the parity bit as the ninth bit: *mark* parity sets it to 1 for control words and *space* parity to 0 for data words [@pyserial]. Before each change of the parity setting, the program waits until the previous bytes have left the adapter.

This method has two side effects that are important for reading the results. The PC reads only the lower 8 bits of each answer, so it prints 0x1B0 as `B0`, 0x180 as `80` and 0x176 as `76`. And the parity changes cost time on the PC side, so the words of one packet arrive in groups, about 2 µs apart inside a group and 1 ms to 2.6 ms apart between groups. The nodes do not depend on the time between words, so these gaps change nothing in the result. They only make the packets longer on the oscilloscope.

The program first sends Count Segments, `160 | 00 | 176`, and then an LED packet with the values in @tbl-pc-values. Just before the LED packet, it sends a broken packet `100 | 20 | 30` without an EOP, to check that a node drops an unfinished packet when a new SOP arrives (@sec-error-handling).

| **Node** | **Red**  | **Green** | **Blue** | **White** |
|:---------|---------:|----------:|---------:|----------:|
| GM1      | 65,535   | 32,767    | 49,151   | 40,000    |
| GM2      | 10,000   | 25,000    | 40,000   | 65,000    |

: Brightness values sent by the PC test program {#tbl-pc-values}

## Communication Tests {#sec-hw-communication}

The PC only shows what comes back to it. To see what really happens between the nodes, the four channels of the oscilloscope were connected to the four serial pins of GM1. Channel A was connected to pin 1 (PC → GM1), B to pin 2 (GM1 → PC), C to pin 3 (GM1 → GM2) and D to pin 4 (GM2 → GM1). The serial decoder of PicoScope decoded the words at 1 MBaud with 9 data bits.

A screenshot of the oscilloscope shows one view. For the serial tests, the raw data was used instead. In PicoScope 7, every capture was exported to the hard drive as CSV files. These are the voltage samples of all four channels at 10 MS/s (one sample every 0.1 µs), and the table of the serial decoder with the value, start time and end time of every word. These CSV files were then read and plotted with a short Python script, using the libraries NumPy and Matplotlib. All plots of the serial lines in this chapter (@fig-hw-decoded, @fig-hw-forwarding, @fig-hw-timing-stats, @fig-count-errors and @fig-led-errors) and all timing values derived from them were made in this way. 

The expected behaviour follows from the design. After programming, both nodes have the ID 0xFF. Count Segments gives GM1 the ID 00, GM1 forwards the value 01, and GM2 takes it as its ID. In the LED packet, GM1 keeps the first eight data bytes and forwards the next eight, and both nodes answer with their ID and the fixed temperature value 0x28. GM1 sends its own answer first and then passes on the answer of GM2 (@sec-downlink).

| **Packet sent by the PC**                    | **Expected answer (as printed by the PC)** | **Measured on GM1 pin 2 (raw data)**     |
|:---------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Count: `160 00 176`                          | `B0 00 76 B0 01 76`                        | `1B0 000 176 1B0 001 176`                |
| LED: `100 20 30` + `100` + 16 bytes + `176`  | `80 00 28 76 80 01 28 76`                  | `180 000 028 176 180 001 028 176`        |

: Answers of the two nodes to the PC test program {#tbl-comm-results}

@fig-hw-decoded shows the result on all four lines. In panel (a), GM1 receives the count value 000 and sends 001 to GM2. In panel (b), both nodes answer: GM2 sends `1B0 001 176` on line D, and GM1 sends its own answer followed by the answer of GM2 on line B, without a gap. Panel (c) shows the forwarding of the LED data: 16 bytes arrive on line A, and only the last eight, `027` to `0E8`, leave on line C. Panel (d) shows the eight answer words of the LED packet. All answers agree with @tbl-comm-results, and the broken packet before the LED packet caused no wrong value and no extra answer. On the boards, the ID LEDs changed from 1111 to 0000 on GM1 and to 0001 on GM2, and the external LEDs took the brightness values of @tbl-pc-values.

![Decoded Flexlink words on the four lines at GM1, plotted with Python from the CSV export of the raw voltage samples (10 MS/s) and of the decoder table (capture `LedData_Valid`). Lanes from top to bottom follow the signal path: A (PC → GM1), C (GM1 → GM2), D (GM2 → GM1), B (GM1 → PC). Values are 9-bit words in hexadecimal. Words above 0xFF are control words.](images/ch6_plot_decoded_packets){#fig-hw-decoded width=100%}

The raw data also confirms the data rate. When a node sends several words in a row, the time from one start bit to the next is one word. The transmitter sends 11 bits of 50 clock cycles and starts the next word two clock cycles after it becomes free, so

$$
T_\text{word} = (11 \cdot 50 + 2) \cdot T_\text{clk} = 552 \cdot 20\ \text{ns} = 11.04\ \mu\text{s}
$$ {#eq-hw-word-time}

In all captures, 144 such word pairs were found. @fig-hw-timing-stats (b) shows their spacing: 90 pairs at 11.0 µs, 48 at 11.1 µs and 6 at 11.2 µs, with a mean of 11.04 µs. The decoder gives times in steps of 0.1 µs, so the single values fall on this grid, but their mean is exactly the value of @eq-hw-word-time. Without the two gap cycles, one bit lasts $(11.04\ \mu\text{s} - 2 \cdot 20\ \text{ns}) / 11 = 1.00\ \mu\text{s}$, so the nodes send at 1 MBaud, as Flexlink requires (R8 in @tbl-requirements).

## Daisy-Chain Test and Forwarding Delay {#sec-hw-chain}

With cut-through forwarding, GM1 can send a word on only after its receiver has accepted it, in the middle of the stop bit, 10.5 bit times after the start edge. A few clock cycles for the synchronizer, the decoder, the FIFO and the transmitter follow:

$$
t_\text{fwd} \approx 10.5 \cdot T_\text{bit} + n \cdot T_\text{clk}
$$ {#eq-fwd-delay}

In the simulation of the final code, the delay is 10.65 µs, so $n \approx 7.5$ clock cycles or about 0.15 µs.

@fig-hw-forwarding shows the LED SOP 0x100 on both sides of GM1, plotted from the raw samples. The word starts on line C 10.7 µs after it started on line A, just after the middle of the stop bit of the received word, as @eq-fwd-delay predicts.

![Forwarding delay of GM1 for the SOP word 0x100, plotted with Python from the CSV export of the raw voltage samples (capture `LedData_Valid`, buffer 2). Line A is the word arriving at GM1, line C the same word leaving towards GM2. The forwarded word starts 10.7 µs after the received one, just after the middle of its stop bit.](images/ch6_plot_forwarding_delay){#fig-hw-forwarding width=100%}

One word does not show whether the delay is really fixed. The script therefore found every forwarded word in all captures recorded at 10 MS/s, 96 words in total, and measured the time between the falling start edges, interpolated between the samples at the decoder threshold of 1.1 V. @fig-hw-timing-stats (a) shows the result. All 96 values lie between 10.61 µs and 10.72 µs, with a mean of 10.69 µs. The spread of about 0.1 µs is as large as the sample interval of the oscilloscope and a few clock cycles of 20 ns. The latter is expected, because the PC and GM1 have independent clocks, so the start edge can fall anywhere within one clock cycle of GM1. The mean agrees with the simulated 10.65 µs within this spread. The delay therefore does not depend on the packet type, the data or the time between packets.

![Timing evaluated with Python from the CSV files of all captures. (a) Forwarding delay of GM1 for 96 forwarded words, from the interpolated start edges on lines A and C. (b) Start-to-start time of two answer words sent back to back on lines B and D, from the decoder table (0.1 µs steps).](images/ch6_plot_timing_stats){#fig-hw-timing-stats width=100%}

The decoder data also shows how the answers travel back (@tbl-hw-timing). GM2 forwards and answers with the same 10.7 µs as GM1, as expected for the same bitstream (R6 in @tbl-requirements). 

| **Compared times**                                  | **Count packet** | **LED packet**  | **Meaning**                                       |
|:----------------------------------------------------|-----------------:|----------------:|:--------------------------------------------------|
| Same word on A and on C                             | 10.7 µs          | 10.7 µs         | cut-through forwarding in GM1                     |
| EOP on A to the first answer word of GM1 on B       | 10.7 µs          | 10.7 µs         | GM1 answers directly after the EOP                |
| EOP on C to the first answer word of GM2 on D       | 10.7 µs          | 10.7 µs         | GM2 has the same timing as GM1                    |
| Answer of GM2 on D to the same answer on B          | 22.4 µs          | 33.5 µs         | GM2's answer waits in the FIFO of GM1             |

: Time differences between the four lines at GM1, from the decoder table (capture `LedData_Valid`) {#tbl-hw-timing}

The waiting time of GM2's answer in GM1 can be calculated. GM2's answer arrives 10.7 µs after GM1 has started its own answer of three words (count) or four words (LED), so it waits $3 \cdot 11\ \mu\text{s} - 10.7\ \mu\text{s} \approx 22.3\ \mu\text{s}$ or $4 \cdot 11\ \mu\text{s} - 10.7\ \mu\text{s} \approx 33.3\ \mu\text{s}$. The measured 22.4 µs and 33.5 µs agree within one sample interval. GM1 therefore always sends its own answer first, and the answers reach the master in the order of the chain (R9 and R18 in @tbl-requirements, @sec-downlink).

A second test showed directly that the position of a board in the chain does not matter. In the normal setup the PC sends to GM1, and GM2 receives its data through GM1. For the test the PC was connected to GM2 instead, and GM2 passed the data on to GM1. No new bitstream was loaded. In both cases the LEDs of the second board showed the colours sent by the PC, and in the second one GM1 received its data through GM2. A board therefore does not need to know whether it is the first or the last node, which is what R6 asks for.

With the measured delay, the time for a full chain can be calculated. An LED packet for 25 segments has 1 SOP, 200 data words and 1 EOP, so 202 words. With @eq-req-t-ct, the last of 25 nodes has its data after

$$
t_\text{total} = 202 \cdot 11\ \mu\text{s} + 24 \cdot 10.69\ \mu\text{s}
= 2222\ \mu\text{s} + 257\ \mu\text{s} \approx 2.48\ \text{ms}
$$ {#eq-total-delay-25}

This is about one tenth of the 25 ms limit. Almost all of this time is the packet itself, and the 24 hops add only 0.26 ms. The evaluation against the requirement follows in @sec-evaluation.

## PWM Measurements {#sec-hw-pwm}

The second part is the PWM. Three questions had to be answered on the hardware. Is the frequency right? Does the on-time follow the value with a step of one clock cycle? Do the values 0 and 65,535 give a signal that is always off and always on? For each value, the red channel of GM1 was set with the PC program, and `seg1` (pin 7) was measured with channel A, with the driver stage connected. Unlike the serial captures, these measurements were taken with the automatic measurements and the rulers of PicoScope, and no raw data was exported.

The counter runs at 50 MHz from 0 to 65,535, so the period is $65{,}536 \cdot 20\ \text{ns} = 1.311\ \text{ms}$ and the frequency 762.9 Hz (@eq-pwm-frequency). The output is high while the counter is below the value $v$, so

$$
t_\text{on} = v \cdot T_\text{clk} = v \cdot 20\ \text{ns}
$$ {#eq-pwm-on-time}

The measured frequency is 763.0 Hz (@fig-hw-pwm-freq). Since one period has exactly 65,536 clock cycles, this also measures the system clock: $65{,}536 \cdot 763.0\ \text{Hz} \approx 50.00\ \text{MHz}$. The serial data gave the same clock through the bit time of 1 µs (@eq-hw-word-time). Two independent measurements thus confirm that the PLL runs at the planned 50 MHz. @tbl-pwm-results compares the on-times.

| **Value $v$** | **Duty cycle $D$** | **Expected $t_\text{on}$** | **Measured $t_\text{on}$** | **Deviation** | 
|--------------:|-------------------:|---------------------------:|---------------------------:|--------------:|
| 0             | 0 %                | always off                 | always off                 | —             |
| 1             | 0.0015 %           | 20 ns                      | 20.15 ns                   | +0.8 %        |
| 10            | 0.015 %            | 200 ns                     | 199.9 ns                   | −0.05 %       |
| 66            | 0.10 %             | 1.320 µs                   | 1.318 µs                   | −0.15 %       |
| 1,000         | 1.5 %              | 20.00 µs                   | 20.00 µs                   | 0.0 %         |
| 10,000        | 15.3 %             | 200.0 µs                   | 200.0 µs                   | 0.0 %         |
| 20,000        | 30.5 %             | 400.0 µs                   | 400.0 µs                   | 0.0 %         |
| 65,534        | 99.997 %           | off for 40 ns per period   | one short drop per period  | —             |
| 65,535        | 100 %              | always on                  | always on                  | —             |

: Expected and measured on-time of the PWM output for different brightness values {#tbl-pwm-results}

The on-times follow @eq-pwm-on-time from 20 ns to 400 µs. The value 1 gives a single pulse of about 20 ns (@fig-hw-pwm-1), which proves that the smallest step is one clock cycle and that the full 16-bit resolution reaches the pin. The small deviations of the short pulses come from placing the rulers by hand on rounded edges. This rounding is a limit of the measurement. The oscilloscope has a bandwidth of 20 MHz, and with the rule of thumb $t_r \approx 0.35 / \text{bandwidth}$ its rise time is about 17.5 ns [@keysight_risetime; @pico_a3000_guide], almost as long as the pulse.

::: {#fig-hw-pwm layout-ncol=1}

![Value 1: one pulse of about 20 ns, measured with rulers.](images/picoscope/PWM_16Bit_1_withRulers.png){#fig-hw-pwm-1 width=85%}

![Value 65,534: the output is high for the whole period except two clock cycles. This 40 ns low phase is the short drop to 0 V at 0 ms and again one period later at 1.31 ms. At 50 MS/s it is only two samples wide, so it looks like a thin line. The measured frequency is 763.0 Hz.](images/picoscope/PWM_16Bit_65534_withFreq.png){#fig-hw-pwm-freq width=85%}

PWM output `seg1` of GM1 at the two ends of the range, measured with the PicoScope 4444.
:::

The second image shows the other end of the range. With the value 65,534, the counter is below the value for 65,534 of the 65,536 clock cycles, so the output is low only while the counter is 65,534 or 65,535, for $2 \cdot 20\ \text{ns} = 40\ \text{ns}$ in each period of 1.31 ms. The oscilloscope shows this as a thin drop to 0 V once per period, and the time between two drops gives the measured frequency of 763.0 Hz. The automatic duty-cycle measurement shows 100.00 %, because the real value of $65{,}534 / 65{,}536 = 99.997\ \%$ is rounded. The thin drop is the proof that 65,534 is still a switching PWM, while 65,535 gives a constant high level.

Between these two ends, @fig-hw-pwm-mid shows two values from the middle of the range. With the value 20,000, the output is on for 400 µs and off for the rest of the 1.31 ms period, and PicoScope measures a pulse width of 400.0 µs. The close-up of the value 66 shows a single pulse of 1.32 µs, which PicoScope measures as 1.320 µs. At this time scale, the shape of the high level also becomes visible.

::: {#fig-hw-pwm-mid layout-ncol=1}

![Value 20,000: on for 400 µs in every period of 1.31 ms (automatic pulse width measurement: 400.0 µs).](images/picoscope/PWM_16Bit_20000.png){#fig-hw-pwm-20000 width=85%}

![Value 66, close-up at 200 ns/div: one pulse of 1.32 µs (automatic pulse width measurement: 1.320 µs). The level rises to about 1.9 V and then falls towards about 1.5 V during the pulse.](images/picoscope/PWM_16Bit_66_CloseUp.png){#fig-hw-pwm-66 width=85%}

PWM output `seg1` of GM1 for two values in the middle of the range, measured with the PicoScope 4444.
:::

One result was not expected. For long pulses, the high level of `seg1` is only about 1.3 V, with a short peak of about 1.9 V after each rising edge (@fig-hw-pwm-20000, @fig-hw-pwm-66). To find the cause, the pin was measured once without and once with the driver stage. Without it, the high level was 2.1 V, and with it, 1.3 V. The only steady load of the driver stage is the 10 kΩ pull-down, which draws about 0.13 mA. A drop of 0.8 V at such a small current points to a high internal resistance in the output path, most likely the bus switch between the FPGA and the Pmod connector (@sec-gatemate). This level is important for the MOSFET, whose threshold lies between 0.8 V and 3.0 V [@onsemi_bs170], and it is discussed in the next section.

The PWM generator therefore works as designed. At 763 Hz it meets the Bronze (400 Hz) and Silver (600 Hz) levels, but not Gold (1 kHz) (@tbl-requirements), and it has a step of 20 ns and clear always-off and always-on states.

## Driver Stage Measurements {#sec-hw-driver}

In a first test, LEDs connected directly to the segment outputs did not light up, especially blue and white, which need about 3 V or more (@sec-led-basics), while the outputs give at most 2.5 V (@sec-gatemate). Each output therefore drives a BS170 as a low-side switch (@sec-low-side-switching, @fig-hw-driver). The series resistor was sized with @eq-series-resistor for about 20 mA from 12 V, which gives 430 Ω to 495 Ω for the four colours (@tbl-driver-values). Since these values lie close together, one value of 470 Ω was used for all channels, which keeps the build simple and gives currents between 18.3 mA and 21.1 mA.

![Driver stage of one channel as built on the breadboard. The FPGA output drives the gate of the BS170 through 100 Ω, and 10 kΩ keeps the gate low when the pin is not driven. The series resistor $R$ is 470 Ω for all four colours (@tbl-driver-values).](images/ch6_driver_stage){#fig-hw-driver width=55%}

| **Part / value**                                  | **Red**       | **Green**     | **Blue**      | **White**     |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|
| LED supply $V_S$                                  | 12 V          | 12 V          | 12 V          | 12 V          |
| Typical forward voltage $V_F$                     | 2.1 V [@avago_hlmp_hx64] | 3.2 V [@avago_hlmp_hx64] | 3.2 V [@avago_hlmp_hx64] | 3.4 V [@maxim2004] |
| Resistor for 20 mA, $(V_S - V_F) / 20\ \text{mA}$ | 495 Ω         | 440 Ω         | 440 Ω         | 430 Ω         |
| Series resistor $R$ used                          | 470 Ω         | 470 Ω         | 470 Ω         | 470 Ω         |
| LED current with 470 Ω (@eq-series-resistor)      | 21.1 mA       | 18.7 mA       | 18.7 mA       | 18.3 mA       |

| Gate pull-down resistor                           | 10 kΩ         | 10 kΩ         | 10 kΩ         | 10 kΩ         |

: Component values of the driver stage {#tbl-driver-values}

The BS170 suits the FPGA because it needs no steady gate current, only the charge of at most 60 pF at each edge, and it carries up to 500 mA, far more than 20 mA [@onsemi_bs170]. Its weak point here is the gate voltage. With the driver stage connected, the gate sees only about 1.3 V (@sec-hw-pwm), below the typical threshold of 2.0 V, and a part with a threshold near 3.0 V would not switch on at all [@onsemi_bs170]. The parts in the prototype switch, and all four LEDs light up and follow the values sent by the PC, but this operating point is not guaranteed by the datasheet. The drain voltage and the LED current were not measured, so the currents in @tbl-driver-values are calculated values. A product would drive the gate with a level shifter or use a MOSFET specified at 2.5 V or lower. Current regulation and the 18 V to 36 V supply belong to the analog side of the AES concept are outside the scope of this thesis (@sec-requirements).

## Robustness Tests {#sec-hw-robustness}

A lighting system in an aircraft must not react to a broken packet with a wrong colour or a wrong ID. For both commands, Count Segments and LED data, the tests therefore first checked the correct result and then sent packets with one thing changed at a time, such as a value, a length or a control word. The answers were compared with the answers of the simulation of the final code. The tests follow the numbering of the test plan. Group A uses correct packets, B checks Count Segments, C checks LED data and D the timing. @tbl-robustness at the end of this section lists all tests that were measured on the hardware. As in @sec-hw-communication, every result was taken from the raw data of its capture, and the figures were plotted from it. The raw data of all captures (voltage samples and decoder tables as CSV), the original PicoScope files and the Python scripts used for the plots are available in the repository of this thesis, in the folders `GateMate-FPGA-Projects/Picoscope_outputs/Final_outputs` (raw data) and `GateMate-FPGA-Projects/Picoscope_outputs/ch6_plots` (decoder tables and the script `make_ch6_plots.py`).

### Count Segments: Correct Result and Wrong Packets {#sec-hw-rob-count}

The correct result (A1) was already shown in @fig-hw-decoded (a) and (b): GM1 takes the count value 00 as its ID, forwards 01 to GM2, and both nodes answer in the order of the chain. A Count Segments packet is accepted only if it has exactly one count value, so the tests of group B check this rule from both sides. They ran one after another, and the LED packet sent after each test shows in its answers whether a node changed its ID.

The first case is a correct packet at the edge of the value range. In test B2, the PC sends the count value 0xFE (@fig-count-errors (a) and (b)). GM1 takes 0xFE as its ID and forwards 0xFF, and both nodes answer with these IDs. The LED packet after the test confirms the IDs 0xFE and 0xFF. The next value, 0xFF, is a special case (test B1). GM1 takes the ID 0xFF and answers, but it does not forward a count value, because 0xFF + 1 would wrap around to 0x00 and give a second node the ID 00. GM2 therefore receives no count value, keeps its old ID and stays silent. Since 0xFF also means "not counted yet", one byte can count at most 255 segments. On the hardware, GM1 forwarded only the SOP 0x160 in this test, without the EOP, and GM2 again did not answer, which is the same result as in the simulation.

The other tests send wrong packets. In test B5, the count value is replaced by the control word 0x150 (@fig-count-errors (c) and (d)). Because of cut-through forwarding, GM1 cannot know in advance that the packet is wrong, so it passes the word on unchanged. When the EOP arrives, neither node has a valid count value, so neither answers, and line B and line D stay idle. Packets with two count values (B3), with no count value (B4) and without an EOP (B7) give the same result. The words are forwarded as they arrive, in B3 with the first value replaced by 01, but no node changes its ID and no node answers. In the LED packets after these tests, both nodes still answer with the ID 0xFF, the value they kept since test B1.

![Count Segments tests at the boundary and with a wrong packet, plotted with Python from the CSV export of the raw data. (a, b) Test B2 (capture `CountSegmentsFE`): GM1 receives the count value 0xFE, forwards 0xFF, and both nodes answer. (c, d) Test B5 (capture `CountSegmentsInvalidSopAsData`): the control word 0x150 instead of a count value is forwarded unchanged, and no node answers. Lanes as in @fig-hw-decoded.](images/ch6_plot_count_errors){#fig-count-errors width=100%}

### LED Data: Correct Result and Wrong Packets {#sec-hw-rob-led}

The correct result (A2) was shown in @fig-hw-decoded (c) and (d): GM1 keeps the first eight data bytes, forwards the next eight, and both nodes answer. The same result was measured in test C2, where the PC first sends the unfinished packet `100 20 30`. GM1 keeps the two bytes without forwarding them, drops them when the new SOP arrives and then handles the new packet normally.

The first group of changed packets are packets that are shorter than the chain needs. In test C5, the PC sends only twelve data bytes (@fig-led-errors (a) and (b)). GM1 keeps the first eight and forwards only the last four, `027` to `0A8`. GM2 receives fewer than the eight bytes it needs, keeps its old values and stays silent, while GM1 answers with `180 000 028 176`. Test C1, with only eight data bytes, behaves in the same way, with no data byte on line C at all. A short packet therefore updates only the first nodes, and the master can see from the number of answers which nodes have taken the new data.

The second group are broken packets. In test C9, the control word 0x110 appears in the middle of the LED data (@fig-led-errors (c) and (d)). GM1 ends the packet at this word and forwards it, together with all following data bytes and the EOP, unchanged to GM2. GM2 applies the same rule, so neither node takes the data and neither answers. A packet with only two data bytes (C6) is also ignored by both nodes. C2 and C9 were recorded at 2 ms/div, so the oscilloscope sampled at 5 MS/s instead of 10 MS/s. With five samples per bit, the decoded values still agree with the values sent by the PC.

![LED data tests with a short and with a broken packet, plotted with Python from the CSV export of the raw data. (a, b) Test C5 (capture `LedData_12Bytes`): of twelve data bytes, GM1 keeps eight and forwards four, and only GM1 answers. (c, d) Test C9 (capture `LedData_InvalidSopAsData`, 5 MS/s): the control word 0x110 inside the data is forwarded, and no node answers. Lanes as in @fig-hw-decoded.](images/ch6_plot_led_errors){#fig-led-errors width=100%}

One kind of error cannot be detected. If a packet has the right format but its data is shifted by one byte, GM2 takes the wrong bytes and still answers. The present design cannot detect this, because the packet has no checksum. This case was not tested on the hardware, and a checksum is discussed as an extension in @sec-outlook.

### Summary of the Tests {#sec-hw-rob-summary}

In all measured tests, the hardware gave the same answers as the simulation of the final code (@tbl-robustness). A wrong or broken packet never changed an ID or a brightness value, and the missing answer tells the master that the packet did not arrive.

| A2      | Normal LED data                   | `100` + 16 bytes + `176`                        | `180 00 28 176 180 01 28 176`     | as expected; GM2 gets bytes 9–16                   | PASS       |
| B1      | Count value 0xFF                  | `160 FF 176`                                    | `1B0 FF 176`, GM2 silent          | as expected; 0xFF not forwarded; IDs after: FF, FF | PASS       |
| B2      | Count value 0xFE                  | `160 FE 176`                                    | `1B0 FE 176 1B0 FF 176`           | as expected; GM1 forwards 0xFF; IDs after: FE, FF  | PASS       |

## Problems and Solutions {#sec-problems}

Several problems came up during the bring-up, and most of them taught something about where errors really come from. In the tool flow, nextpnr stopped with "Pad not available" because `dn_tx` and `up_tx` were assigned twice in the constraint file, and Yosys stopped with a syntax error (`TOK_ELSE`) after a second `else` branch was added to the decoder. Both were fixed in the source files. A logic error made the LED answer one word too short, because the index of the last answer word was still set for the three-word count answer. The simulation failed after the change to 1 MBaud, because the testbench still used the bit time of 115,200 baud.

Other problems came from the PC side. The test program failed with `ModuleNotFoundError: serial` when it was started in the window of the build script, which uses the Python of the OSS CAD Suite, and openFPGALoader programmed the wrong board until each board was selected by its serial number. The gaps of 1 ms to 2.6 ms between groups of words also come from the PC, which changes the parity setting before each group. They were accepted, because the nodes do not depend on the time between words.

The electrical problems were the direct LED connection, which failed because of the 2.5 V output level and led to the BS170 driver stage (@sec-hw-driver), and the high level of only 1.3 V with the driver stage connected (@sec-hw-pwm), which was accepted for the prototype but needs a level shifter in a product.

The main lesson is that the PC side can hide or cause errors that look like errors of the FPGA design. The gaps between the words and the missing ninth bit in the printed answers both come from the PC and the adapter. Only the oscilloscope with its raw data made it possible to separate the behaviour of the nodes from the behaviour of the PC.

In summary, the node forwards every word after a fixed delay of 10.69 µs, independent of the data, so a chain of 25 segments is updated in about 2.5 ms. It generates the PWM at 763 Hz with steps of 20 ns, and it answers correctly and in the order of the chain, while broken packets are ignored. It does this with less than 2 % of the FPGA, at 50 MHz with 5.5 ns of timing margin, and with the same bitstream on every board. The evaluation of these results against the requirements follows in @sec-evaluation.
